questions.question: Define excretion, distinguish it from egestion, and name the three excretory organs with the waste each removes.
questions.expected_answer: Excretion is the removal of waste products made by the chemical reactions of the body's cells, such as carbon dioxide and urea. Egestion is the removal of undigested food as faeces, material that never entered the body's cells or blood. Lungs excrete carbon dioxide (and water vapour); skin excretes water and salts in sweat; kidneys excrete urea, excess water and excess salts as urine.

questions.question: Describe the two processes by which the kidney produces urine, stating which substances are filtered, which stay in the blood, and which are reabsorbed.
questions.expected_answer: Filtration: blood under high pressure in the capillaries of the nephron forces small molecules, water, glucose, salts and urea, into the nephron tube; blood cells and proteins are too large and stay in the blood (about 180 litres of filtrate per day). Reabsorption: the tube wall takes back into the blood all the glucose, about 99 percent of the water and the salts the body needs; urea is left behind. The remaining fluid, about 1,5 litres per day of water with urea and excess salts, is urine.

questions.question: Explain how the kidneys respond on a hot day after heavy sweating, and describe how dialysis keeps a person with kidney failure alive.
questions.expected_answer: Sweating removes water so the blood becomes more concentrated; the brain detects this and releases a hormone making the kidneys reabsorb more water, so a small volume of dark concentrated urine is produced and the person feels thirsty. In dialysis the patient's blood flows through a machine alongside a special fluid, separated by a membrane that lets urea, excess salts and water pass out but keeps blood cells and proteins; about four hours, three times a week, replaces the filtering the failed kidneys cannot do.
